newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government aims at 2.3 percent 1997 growth.
newsitem.headline: French government aims at 2.3 percent 1997 growth.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Friday the 1997 budget due to be announced this month would forecast economic growth at 2.3 percent next year.

"The growth assumption which I have retained is 2.3 percent," he told a news conference the day after the government unveiled income tax cuts designed to snap the country out of its mood of pessimism.
Arthuis also stuck with his growth forecast of 1.3 percent for this year.

The government said on Thursday that over five years it planned to bring the top rate of income tax down to 47 percent from 56.8, and increase the threshold before people start paying tax to help the lower paid.
It said it would cut income taxes by 25 billion francs ($4.9 billion) next year, although part of that will be recouped through heavier taxation elsewhere.
Arthuis told reporters the 1997 budget would increase taxes on alcohol and tobacco to help fund the welfare system. Petrol duties would be increased in line with inflation.
He declined to say how much money would be raised through the extra taxes, but Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure said these would raise a "significant sum".

Arthuis said on radio that the Generalised Social Contribution (CSG), a flat tax on most income that funds welfare spending and is being increased to 3.4 percent from 2.4, would also be extended to stock dividends.

Asked about the extension of the CSG announced as part of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's tax overhaul, Arthuis said: "There are...some revenues subject to the flat tax on investment income and others on dividends which are not covered by this tax. There will be an extension this time."

Officials have said the aim of the tax changes is to lift consumer spending, stalled by worries about record unemployment, and to underpin an economic recovery that is meant to take France into European monetary union.
